\chapter{Review --- One Question, Three Answers}
\label{ch:review-two-pasts}
\hlchaptermodality{97}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can state the single question that chooses between the two past tenses.}

Complete ES-C48-repaso-dos-pasados: state the question, identify the scene verb, and name the pair that changes meaning.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Review — one question, three answers}

\label{lesson:ES-C48-repaso-dos-pasados}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new. Before the table: do the two past tenses differ in \textbf{when}?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three chapters, one question, three ways it gets answered.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you are doing} & \textbf{tense} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
reporting an event, with edges & \textbf{preterite} & \emph{hablé} — I spoke \\
setting a scene, no edges & \textbf{imperfect} & \emph{hablaba} — I was speaking \\
naming a state & \textbf{imperfect} & \emph{tenía} — I had \\
naming the moment a state began & \textbf{preterite} & \emph{tuve} — I got \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Rows one and two are the same event seen from two places. Rows three and four are not: there the tense changes what happened.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the question to actually ask}]
Not \emph{\textquotedblleft{}which tense is this?\textquotedblright{}} — that has no answer without you.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Am I telling you what happened, or what things were like?}
\end{quote}

\emph{What happened} has edges: preterite. \emph{What things were like} does not: imperfect. A story is mostly the second with the first dropped into it, which is what \emph{cuando} let you build:

\begin{quote}
\emph{Estudiaba cuando habló Ana.}
\end{quote}

And when the verb names a state rather than an action, the same question still works — you are simply more likely to be describing what things were like, so the imperfect is the ordinary case and the preterite is the special one.

There is no list to memorise here, and that is deliberate. Lists of \textquotedblleft{}preterite trigger words\textquotedblright{} exist in most courses and they fail exactly where the choice is interesting, because the same word can sit in either sentence. The question does not fail, because the question is the thing the language is actually asking.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hablé / hablaba\textquotedblright{}, then \textquotedblleft{}tenía / tuve\textquotedblright{}, and name the difference in each pair
  \item the question aloud before each one
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Until the question arrives before the verb does.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The one question? (\textbf{What happened}, or \textbf{what things were like}?) Which pair changes meaning rather than viewpoint? (\emph{\textbf{Tenía}} and \emph{\textbf{tuve}}.) Next: a whole small story, which is what all of this was for.
\end{tcolorbox}
